newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. chief alarmed over refugees in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.N. chief alarmed over refugees in Zaire.

text.p: U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan asked the five permanent Security Council members on Friday to warn Zaire and its neighbors not to turn a huge refugee camp into a battleground, U.N. officials said.
The request was given to envoys the United States, Britain, France, China and Russia and diplomats said they would convey the warning to the governments of Zaire, Rwanda and Uganda.

At risk are 150,000 Rwandan refugees in the makeshift Tingi Tingi camps in eastern Zaire. Former Hutu Rwandan soldiers and militia in the settlement are receiving weapons, ammunition and uniforms, presumably from the Zairian army in its battle against rebel forces, the United Nations said.
The Rwandan Hutu refugees and soldiers in the camps fled their homeland, fearing reprisals after the 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis by hardline Hutus.

Both Rwanda and Uganda have ties to the Tutsi-led rebels in Zaire who revolted against the Kinshasa government in October. The rebels hold major towns and territory along the border with Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda.

Annan did not mention his request to the five countries but appealed to all parties "to stop turning the refugee camp into an armed base and to ensure the safety and security of all refugees and humanitarian personnel."

The diplomats said Sadako Ogata, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, who visited Tingi Tingi over the weekend, had indications that rebel forces were preparing to launch an offensive against the encampment, where doctors say hunger and disease is killing up to 30 people a day.
Relief agencies pulled foreign staff out of Tingi Tingi on Friday, saying panicky Zairian troops fired in the air and demanded money and vehicles from them.
Annan, in his statement, said he told the five ambassadors of his "deep concern" about "the militarization of the main refugee encampment near Tingi-Tingi."
He said that Rwandan soldiers and militias in the settlement were receiving weapons and ammunitions by air and were being sent to frontlines.

"Military elements are being deployed in positions near the camps and sections of the encampment are being used as storage facilities for arms and ammunition," he said, adding that young male refugees were being actively recruited.
"This situation puts at risk the lives of innocent refugees and humanitarian workers in the area," he said.
U.N. officials said that Mohammed Sahnoun, the new special envoy for Central Africa, would convey Annan's warnings to the Kinasha government when he arrives in Zaire on Saturday.
The war was launched by ethnic Tutsis, who accused the Zairean authorities of denying them citizenship and of plans to expel them to neighboring Rwanda, their ancestral home.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said he had ordered his forces to avoid the Tingi Tingi camp. But diplomats said the military buildu in and around the encampments might result in such an attack anyway.
Kabila has said that President Mobutu Sese Seko, who has spent most of the last year in France recovering from surgery, should begin talks by Feb. 21 on stepping down.
